PERFORMANCE.html.summary: Performance How ParquetNeo compares with Parquet.Net (6.1.0) and ParquetSharp (25.0.1.2, a wrapper of the Apache Arrow C++ implementation), and what was done about what the measurements showed. What is measured One dataset of 1,000,000 rows and five columns: a required long, a nullable string with 5,000 distinct values (one null in ten), a nullable double (one null in three), a required int in a small range and a required bool. It is written as one row group, with the default encodings of each library (dictionary encoding where the library chooses it), uncompressed and with Snappy, to and from memory. columns: the column-wise API of each library, which is the closest to the file (ParquetFileWriter for ParquetNeo, ParquetWriter for Parquet.Net, ParquetFileWriter with LogicalWriter for ParquetSharp). serializer: objects in, objects out (ParquetSerializer of ParquetNeo and of Parquet.Net). ParquetSharp has none. Reading: every library reads the same file, written by ParquetSharp, into arrays (columns) or into objects (serializer). The competitors are driven the way their own documentation makes fastest, and each choice was timed against the alternatives (1M rows, same machine) before it was kept: ParquetSharp, reading: a native buffer (BufferReader over the pinned bytes) and its physical column readers for the numbers (49 ms with the logical readers over a .NET stream, 38 ms with these, and 36 MB allocated against 8.5 MB). The text columns have no physical form that makes strings, so they use the logical reader. A physical ReadBatch can return fewer values than asked for, so it is called until every row is read (the benchmark checks the count). Parquet.Net, reading: ReadRawAsync for the nullable double, which returns the values and their definition levels the way ParquetNeo does, instead of ReadAsync, which expands them to double? (62–76 ms down to 46–52 ms). ParquetSharp, writing: nothing was faster than the logical writers: physical writers, a native output buffer and switching size statistics off all took 101–105 ms against 103 ms. The column descriptors are made once, outside the timed method. Parquet.Net, writing: nothing was faster either: neither the pool limits, the dictionary settings (none of them make it use a dictionary), nor reusing the fields changed its 73 ms. Every library allocates the arrays it reads into inside the timed method, so none is helped by buffers made in advance. dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/ParquetNeo.Benchmarks -- --filter "*WriteComparison*" dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/ParquetNeo.Benchmarks -- --filter "*ReadComparison*" ColumnBreakdown times each column of the low-level writer and reader on its own, which is how the work below was found. Results BenchmarkDotNet 0.15.8, .NET 10.0.14, Intel Xeon 2.10 GHz, 4 cores, Linux. Mean of 6 iterations after 2 warm-up iterations (a short job, so the error margins are wide: see the notes). Smaller is better. Writing Uncompressed Snappy Allocated File (uncompressed / Snappy) ParquetNeo, columns 67 ms 89 ms 18 KB 16.2 / 8.8 MB ParquetNeo, columns, no dictionary 38 ms 65 ms 13 KB 31.3 / 10.9 MB Parquet.Net, columns 88 ms 123 ms 28 MB 32.7 / 11.0 MB ParquetSharp, columns 112 ms 128 ms 13 MB 15.7 / 8.2 MB ParquetNeo, serializer 129 ms 148 ms 36 MB (20 KB since the pooled buffers, below) 16.2 / 8.8 MB ParquetNeo, serializer, 4 threads 103 ms 107 ms 36 MB same Parquet.Net, serializer 140 ms 166 ms 128 MB 32.7 / 11.0 MB Parquet.Net's column writer writes every column PLAIN, with no dictionary (its dictionary options do not change that), which is cheaper per row and makes its files about twice the size of those of the libraries that use a dictionary. The like-for-like comparison with it is the row of ParquetNeo without a dictionary, which writes the same kind of file (31 MB against 33 MB) in less than half the time uncompressed. dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/ParquetNeo.Benchmarks -- --sizes prints the sizes. Reading Uncompressed Snappy Allocated ParquetNeo, columns 22 ms 44 ms 34 MB Parquet.Net, columns 88 ms 94 ms 73–92 MB ParquetSharp, columns 51 ms 80 ms 30 MB ParquetNeo, serializer 130 ms 145 ms 106 MB Parquet.Net, serializer 210 ms 180 ms 148–167 MB Notes on the numbers They come from one machine, one dataset and a short BenchmarkDotNet job. Differences of 10 to 20 percent between two rows are within the noise (the error column of the BenchmarkDotNet output is up to about 15 ms for writes, and the Parquet.Net serializer read has an error close to its mean). The large differences, such as reading through columns, are not. Writing through columns is ahead of both libraries, and the like-for-like row (no dictionary, the file Parquet.Net writes) is more than twice as fast as Parquet.Net uncompressed. The serializer takes about twice as long as the column API; it is ahead of Parquet.Net's serializer in both directions. ParquetNeo's writer takes its scratch space from the pool, so it allocates next to nothing once it is warm: the figure is for a file written after others, as in a benchmark or a service. A single file written in a fresh process still allocates for the pool to grow the first time. What the measurements led to Timing each column alone (ColumnBreakdown) showed that one column dominated both directions: the dictionary encoded string column took 93% of the time of the reader and 60% of the writer. Hence: Strings of a dictionary are decoded once. Reading text turned every value into a new string, 900,000 of them for 5,000 distinct values. A text dictionary now turns each entry into a string the first time it is used and hands out that string for every row that refers to it. Reading the string column went from 77 ms and 42 MB to 8 ms and 0.25 MB, and the whole table through columns from 108 ms to 23 ms. A batch of text also no longer ends at the end of a page, since the values are copies and no longer point into the page. Strings are encoded in one pass. Up to 1,024 characters, a string is encoded to UTF-8 straight into a buffer sized for the longest it can be, instead of being measured and then encoded. Plain encoded string columns write about 20 percent faster. Statistics of a dictionary column look at new entries only. The minimum and maximum of a column cannot change when a value already in the dictionary comes again, so only values new to the dictionary are compared (900,000 comparisons became 5,000 here). None of this changes the files that are written. A second round went to the serializer, whose profile showed the encoders at about 60% of a write and the shredding of rows at about a third: Columns can be encoded in parallel (MaxDegreeOfParallelism of ParquetSerializerOptions and of ParquetDataWriterOptions; 1, the calling thread, by default). Each column of a row group is encoded into a buffer of its own on a different thread and the buffers are copied to the file in the order of the schema, so the file is the same, byte for byte, whatever the degree. With four threads the serializer writes the table in 128 ms (121 ms with Snappy) instead of 143 ms (162 ms); the time is bounded by the slowest column, here the strings. The column buffers are made big enough up front (the size of the row group, or the number of rows when the collection says how many there are) and no longer grow by doubling and copying. The synchronous serializer writes straight to the stream and no longer stages the file in memory to copy it. A property is read with one delegate call instead of two, and a reference is stored in a buffer without the check an array of references makes. Reading rows sizes its lists and arrays from the file: the list of rows (which was also copied once more into the list that is returned) and the arrays that hold a column. The numbers are those of the file, so they are only trusted up to two million entries and the arrays grow normally beyond that. The serializer writes in 143 ms where it took 198 ms, with 87 MB allocated instead of 188 MB, and reads in 125 ms where it took 186 ms, with 106 MB allocated instead of 162 MB. A third round went to writing through columns, which allocated 52 MB for the table (against 28 MB and 13 MB for the other libraries) and was slower than Parquet.Net on at least one laptop. Writing each column on its own showed where it went: the two columns of unique values (an identifier and an amount) spent 19 ms and 25 MB each building a dictionary of 131,000 entries that the writer then gave up, and the string column spent most of its 47 ms in its dictionary. The dictionaries are open-addressing tables over pooled arrays, for numbers (FixedDictionary) and for byte arrays and strings (BinaryDictionary: the values are copied one after the other into one array, and an entry is its offset, length and hash, so most mismatches are told from the hash alone). Entries are numbered in order of first appearance, so the file is the same. The hash is seeded randomly for every dictionary, so that input chosen by an attacker cannot be crafted to collide. The scratch buffers of a writer come from the pool (PooledBufferWriter, in place of ArrayBufferWriter, which grows by doubling and is made anew for every file) and go back when the file is closed. A dictionary index is appended with one call instead of a request for room and an advance. The unique long column went from 19 ms and 25 MB to 5 ms and nothing; the unique double column from 19 ms and 26 MB to 12 ms; the string column from 47 ms to 37 ms. The table through columns went from 86 ms and 52 MB to 67–71 ms and 18 KB. A fourth round compiled the rows. A row type whose properties are all single columns (no nested objects, collections or maps, and, for reading, created by its parameterless constructor) is written and read by one function generated for it with expression trees, instead of a loop over a tree of small objects that each make a virtual call and call a delegate per value: Writing: the function reads every property of the row and adds it to its column buffer (LeafBuffer), with the null checks that the type of the property needs (none for a value type, HasValue for a nullable one, a reference check for a reference type, and the same error naming the property and the row when a required column is null). Reading: the function creates the instance, takes the next value of every column and sets the property, or sets it to null (or raises the same error naming the row, when it cannot be). Any other shape (nested objects, lists, maps, types built by a constructor) keeps the general path, which does the same thing. The files written are the same, byte for byte. On the 1,000,000-row table of five columns the serializer writes in about 118 ms where it took 142 ms, and reads in about 65 ms where it took about 90 ms (the floor, objects made by hand from arrays read through the column API, is 39 ms). A fifth round gave up on dictionaries sooner, as an option because it changes which files are written. A column of mostly different values (an identifier, a measurement) fills a dictionary up to its size limit (131,000 entries for a long) before the writer gives it up, which cost 5 ms for the identifier column against 1.4 ms written plain, and left a file 7% bigger because of the dictionary page and the pages held for it. DictionaryMode says, for a column, how it is dictionary encoded: Standard (the default, as before), Adaptive or Disabled. It is set for chosen columns with ParquetWriterOptions.ColumnDictionaries (by column path, like ColumnEncodings) or, in the serializer, with [ParquetDictionary(DictionaryMode.Adaptive)] on the property; the options win over the attribute, and DictionaryEnabled = false turns every dictionary off whatever a column says. A size limit per column: DictionarySettings carries the mode and an optional SizeLimit that replaces DictionaryPageSizeLimit for that column (SizeLimit = on [ParquetDictionary], or a DictionarySettings in ColumnDictionaries; a DictionaryMode alone converts to settings). Raise it for a column with few distinct values that are large (long texts, urls), whose dictionary would be dropped half way through; the dictionary and its pages are held in memory until the column is complete, so it costs memory. Adaptive looks at the first 32 KiB of the values of the column (4,096 longs); if more than nine in ten are different, the dictionary is dropped there and the rest is written plain. The dictionary page and page written for those first values stay in the file (32 KB for a long), which readers handle like any other column that gave up its dictionary. A column that repeats is unchanged, byte for byte. On the benchmark table (identifier and amount adaptive; one laptop that was busy, so the ratios are what matters) writing the columns takes 0.80 of the time it did, 1 MB less in the file (16.2 MB to 15.2 MB uncompressed, 8.8 MB to 7.8 MB with Snappy). Written plain, without any dictionary, it takes 0.55 of the time, but the file is twice the size: the remaining difference is the dictionary of the string column. A sixth round went to the string dictionary, whose loop was the hottest in a column of text: The hash is one 64 by 64 bit multiplication for values up to 16 bytes (two overlapping words, in the manner of wyhash) and one per 16 bytes beyond that, in place of a rotate and multiply per 8 bytes. It is still seeded randomly for every dictionary, and the output does not depend on it. ASCII text is narrowed with Ascii.FromUtf16, a vector at a time, and only text that is not ASCII goes through the UTF-8 transcoder. One loop adds a page of strings to the dictionary, keeping what changes in locals (the bytes of the page, the count of values, the dictionary, the statistics) instead of fields that every value reads and writes. The string column of 1,000,000 rows (900,000 values, 5,000 of them different) went from 26–28 ms to 24–25 ms; the table of five columns by 2 to 3 ms of 43 (the measurements of this laptop vary by that much). The files are the same, byte for byte. A seventh round made the parallel form public: RowGroupWriter.WriteColumns(actions, maxDegreeOfParallelism) (and an overload that uses the processors, and a cancellation token) takes one action per column, encodes them on different threads and copies the encoded columns to the file in the order of the schema, which is what the serializer and the ADO.NET writer already did. The file is the same, byte for byte, as the one written a column at a time (tested for several degrees, with and without compression). The encoded group is held in memory until every column is done, which NextColumn does not need. On the benchmark table, through the column API with four threads: 48.7 ms becomes 33.0 ms uncompressed (0.68) and 73.1 ms becomes 34.1 ms with Snappy (0.47); the time is that of the slowest column, here the strings. An eighth round brought the compiled functions to rows that are not flat. The function generated for an object now handles every kind of property: a single column goes straight to its buffer (or is taken from its column), and an object, collection or dictionary is handed to its shredder (or assembler), which is called directly from the generated code instead of through a delegate that reads or sets the property. An object anywhere in the row is compiled, with the definition and repetition levels as arguments because it can be anywhere in the row. When reading, a list that is an array or a List<T> collects its elements in a scratch buffer of the read and is then made once, with exactly the room it needs, in place of a list that grows by doubling (and for an array, is copied again by ToArray); the scratch belongs to the read, not to the assembler, since assemblers are shared by every read of a row type. On 200,000 orders with an optional customer, an address, a list of tags, an array of scores and a list of order lines, written to a memory stream and read back (the NestedSerializerBenchmarks class), the time to write went from 117–131 ms to 104–118 ms, the time to read from 78–91 ms to 71–78 ms, and the memory allocated when reading from 144 MB to 124 MB. Reading is bound by the garbage collector (the objects it creates), so the time improves less than the allocation does. The files are the same, byte for byte. A ninth round pooled the column buffers of the serializer. A row group of a million rows takes about 35 MB of arrays (the values and the levels of each column), and they were allocated for every file written: on the large object heap, so every file caused a full garbage collection or more. A benchmark run on a laptop showed it as Gen2 collections for the serializer with four threads (one for every 16 files) that the column API does not have. LeafBuffer now takes its arrays from the shared array pool and gives them back when the serializer is disposed (cleared, for arrays of references, so that the pool does not keep the rows' strings alive), and so does the buffer of the ADO.NET writer. The pool hands out arrays that are not cleared and may be larger than asked, which nothing here depends on (checked by writing sparse rows into arrays a run of full ones left behind: the file is the same bytes). Per file of the benchmark table, the serializer allocates 20 KB (it was 36 MB) and 27 KB with four threads, with no garbage collection at all in a steady state; the time with four threads went from about 72 ms to 62 ms on the machine of the tests, and the time with one thread is unchanged within the noise of the measurements. The cost is that the pool keeps the arrays between files (it releases them when memory is short), so a process that writes one big file and then nothing holds on to that much memory for a while. A tenth round tuned asynchronous output, which had two costs: the encoded row group was staged in a MemoryStream that doubles on the large object heap for every file, and the next row group was not collected or encoded until the write of the one before had ended, so the time was that of encoding plus that of writing. Now: The staging area is pooled (StagingStream): the bytes of a row group are encoded into arrays from the array pool, and the buffer that follows starts as big as the one before, so a file does not grow its staging by doubling and copying. A row group is written while the next is collected and encoded (PipelinedWriter): WriteAsync of the stream is started and not awaited until the next row group is ready to be handed over, since a stream takes one write at a time. At most two row groups are in memory. A failed or cancelled write surfaces at the next hand-over or at the end, and the memory of a write that is going is not given back to the pool until the write ends. The same for SerializeAsync of asynchronous rows and for the asynchronous ADO.NET writer. The synchronous ADO.NET writer writes straight to the stream, as the synchronous serializer already did, instead of staging each row group in memory first. Four row groups of the benchmark table (4,000,000 rows, 64.7 MB), to a destination that takes the time a given speed would: Destination before after memory stream 394 ms 322 ms 400 MB/s 535 ms 360 ms 200 MB/s 663 ms 435 ms 100 MB/s 1,011 ms 756 ms With a destination that takes no time the gain comes from the pooled staging (97 MB allocated on the calling thread becomes 35 MB, and 0.1 MB with the pooled column buffers of the round before); with a slow one the encoding hides behind the writes (at 100 MB/s the writes alone take about 650 ms). Only the row groups overlap: a file of a single row group has nothing to overlap, so RowGroupSize should be a fraction of the rows for a slow destination. AsyncWriteComparison reproduces it with BenchmarkDotNet. Generated mappings [ParquetSerializable] (step 14) gives a type a mapping written at build time, for trimming and Native AOT. It must not cost time at run time, which GeneratedMappingWriteBenchmarks and GeneratedMappingReadBenchmarks check: the same 100,000 rows as a type with a generated mapping and as a twin left to reflection, flat (eight columns of numbers, text, a date, an enum) and nested (objects, lists, an array and a dictionary inside), to a memory stream and back. Linux x64, one run: reflection generated ratio write, flat 24.0 ms 25.4 ms 1.06 write, nested 70.0 ms 68.3 ms 0.98 read, flat 18.4 ms 17.3 ms 0.94 read, nested 116.1 ms 116.0 ms 1.00 read, flat record 47.5 ms 20.2 ms 0.43 The record row (the same eight columns, created by a constructor with parameters) is the exception, and the one place the generated code is faster: the reflection path holds the values in boxed slots until the constructor is called (35 MB allocated for 100,000 rows), where the generated code calls the constructor with the values straight from the columns (19 MB, the same as for a class). The other differences are inside the error of the runs (the standard deviation of the nested read is 20 ms, since it allocates 92 MB of rows and the time depends on when the garbage collector runs), and the allocation is the same to the byte. The generated code is the same straight-line code the expression compiler made, so parity is the expected result; what the generated mapping removes is the reflection and the compilation when a type is first used, and the need for either with Native AOT. Not done yet Left for a follow-up, with what is known so far: Rows built by a constructor, without a generated mapping. Types that are created by a constructor with parameters (records, for example) still read through the general path when they have no [ParquetSerializable], which holds the values in boxed slots until the constructor is called; a generated mapping calls the constructor with the values straight from the columns (see Generated mappings), and the reflection path could do the same with a compiled function. Collections and dictionaries inside rows are walked by their shredders and assemblers (a virtual call for each element); only the properties around them are compiled. Maps are still created empty and added to. Encoding strings further. The dictionary encoded string column is still the slowest column to write (about 24 ms of the 42 ms for the table, 27 ns for each of 900,000 values). The profile is flat: reading the string objects (they are all over the heap), narrowing them to bytes, hashing, the lookup (a table, an entry, then the bytes) and packing the indexes each take a few nanoseconds. A layout of the entries that puts offset, length and hash side by side was tried and did not show a gain. What would help most is not doing the work for a value: a cache by string reference helps data that shares its strings, but needs a hash of the reference, which the runtime does not give cheaply. Asynchronous input. DeserializeAllAsync reads the footer and the byte ranges of the columns the row type needs; it does not read the next row group while the rows of one are assembled, as the writer now does in the other direction.

PLAN.html.title: ParquetNeo – Implementation Plan | ParquetNeo
PLAN.html.summary: ParquetNeo – Implementation Plan A from-scratch, high-performance Parquet reader/writer for .NET (C#), built from the Parquet format specification and parquet.thrift. Status: steps 0 to 16 are done and the packages are ready to be published with the first v tag. Deferred: the PAR3 footer (15e). Next: step 17 and the enhancements listed after step 15. The Status column of the tables below says which steps are done. Goals Fast first, easy second. Zero per-value allocations on hot paths, span-based APIs, pooled buffers, SIMD where it pays off, async I/O. Two layers of usage Low level (ParquetNeo): ParquetFileReader / ParquetFileWriter work on row groups and column chunks. Columns are read/written as Span<T> plus definition/repetition levels. Metadata and statistics are exposed. High level (ParquetNeo.Serialization, which builds on ParquetNeo): ParquetSerializer.SerializeAsync<T>(...) and DeserializeAsync<T>(...) / IAsyncEnumerable<T> over plain DTOs. Built on top of the low-level layer; users never touch columns. Minimal dependencies. Core depends only on the BCL. Thrift compact protocol and all encodings are hand-written. Gzip/Brotli via System.IO.Compression. Snappy (via the managed Snappier library), Zstd and LZ4_RAW live in optional add-on packages. Tested. Every step ships with TUnit unit tests (see Testing). Decisions / assumptions (change in review if you disagree) Topic Default Target framework net10.0 only (matches the existing scaffold) Encryption (modular) Out of scope for v1 Variant, Variant shredding, Geospatial, ALP After the core is stable (step 17) LZ4 (Hadoop-framed) / LZO Not supported. LZ4_RAW is INT96 Read-only (deprecated but common in the wild) Interop fixtures Files from apache/parquet-testing committed under tests/; pyarrow used to generate extra fixtures only if available Spec points that shape the design Footer may carry extensions at Thrift field id 32767; readers must skip unknown Thrift fields and tolerate trailing extension bytes. PAR3 / FlatBuffers footers are an optional later extra. Writers must emit both LogicalType and legacy ConvertedType; readers fall back to ConvertedType when LogicalType is absent; unknown logical types degrade to the physical type. Dictionary page: at most one per column chunk and always first. Nulls live only in definition levels; required / non-nested columns skip levels entirely. Pages may carry optional CRC32 checksums. Gzip readers must accept multi-member streams. Recommended defaults: ~8 KB data pages, 512 MB–1 GB row groups – both configurable. Working routine For every step below: A branch is created for the step (step-NN-short-name). Work is done there, including tests. A pull request is opened against main. Review and comments happen on GitHub; fixes are pushed to the same branch. Each step is sized to be reviewable on its own (roughly 300–800 lines of production code plus tests). Steps Milestone 1 – Foundations # Step Status Deliverable 0 Scaffold Done Replace xunit with TUnit (Microsoft.Testing.Platform), remove Class1.cs, add .editorconfig, GitHub Actions build + test workflow, empty BenchmarkDotNet project, README skeleton. 1 Thrift compact protocol + metadata Done Span-based compact protocol reader/writer for the subset Parquet needs; generated-by-hand model of FileMetaData, RowGroup, ColumnChunk, ColumnMetaData, PageHeader, SchemaElement, Statistics, LogicalType, etc. from specs/parquet.thrift. Unknown-field skipping and field 32767. Tests: golden bytes, round-trips, metadata from a real file. 2 Schema model Done Schema tree (physical type, repetition, logical annotations); conversion to/from the flattened SchemaElement list; max definition/repetition level computation. Milestone 2 – Flat columns, read and write # Step Status Deliverable 3 Level & primitive encodings Done RLE/bit-packed hybrid (SIMD unpack/pack), PLAIN for all physical types, boolean bit-packing. 4 Compression Done ICodec abstraction; Uncompressed, Gzip (multi-member read) and Brotli built in; Snappy (Snappier), Zstd and LZ4_RAW in add-on packages. 5 Low-level writer (flat) Done PAR1 magic, data page v1, required and optional flat columns, PLAIN, row-group builder, footer. 6 Low-level reader (flat) Done Footer parsing, column chunk/page iteration, read into spans. Tests: files from step 5 and external fixtures. 7 Dictionary encoding Done Dictionary page write/read, RLE_DICTIONARY (and legacy PLAIN_DICTIONARY on read), fallback to PLAIN when the dictionary grows too large. 7b Statistics Done Min/max/null-count statistics per column chunk (type-correct ordering, exact flags), exposed on the metadata. Milestone 3 – Full format coverage # Step Status Deliverable 8 Nested columns Done Repetition levels in the low-level reader and writer: nested schemas, leaf columns written and read with definition and repetition levels, pages that never split a row, row and entry counts. 8b Nested assembly Done Converting between levels and offsets/validity for structs, lists and maps (shredding and assembly), standard LIST/MAP schema builders, and recognition of the legacy LIST/MAP layouts on read. 9 Advanced encodings Done DELTA_BINARY_PACKED, DELTA_LENGTH_BYTE_ARRAY, DELTA_BYTE_ARRAY, BYTE_STREAM_SPLIT in the reader and writer; the writer takes them per column (ColumnEncodings, PLAIN by default). 9b Data page v2 writing Done The writer can produce data page v2 (levels uncompressed, is_compressed, num_rows/num_nulls), chosen by an option; the reader already reads it. 10 Logical types (numbers, time, identifiers) Done Typed read and write overloads on the column reader and writer: sized and unsigned integers, DateOnly, TimeOnly, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, Guid, Half; checks of the column's logical type; ConvertedType written alongside. 10b Logical types (decimal, text, INT96) Done decimal reads and writes for DECIMAL columns of every physical type (scale up to 28, exact: digits are never lost), ReadStrings for STRING/ENUM/JSON (and the annotation check on WriteStrings), read-only INT96 timestamps as DateTime/DateTimeOffset, and the fallback to the physical type for unknown logical types. Larger decimals (BigInteger, wide scales) are left to the high-level API. Milestone 4 – High-level DTO API # Step Status Deliverable 11 High-level write (flat rows) Done ParquetSerializer.Serialize / SerializeAsync (sync, IEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerable<T>) writing rows as a Parquet file: a schema inferred from the public properties (primitives, decimal, strings, binary, Guid, date and time types, Nullable<T> and nullable reference types), attributes to rename, order, ignore, and set decimal precision, time units and encodings, and rows batched into row groups that are encoded and written as they fill. 11b High-level write (nested) Done Nested objects, collections (arrays, List<T>, any IEnumerable<T>), dictionaries and enums as properties, written as groups, LISTs and MAPs through the Dremel levels; nullability from nullable reference types at every level; attributes reaching the elements, keys and values. 12 High-level read (flat rows) Done ParquetSerializer.Deserialize / DeserializeAll / DeserializeAsync / DeserializeAllAsync reading rows into DTOs one row group at a time: columns matched by property name, only those columns read (and, asynchronously, only their byte ranges fetched), clear SchemaMismatchExceptions for missing or mismatched columns, DTOs created through a parameterless constructor or a record-style constructor, enums by name. 12b High-level read (nested) Done Nested objects, collections (arrays, List<T>, sets and other ICollection<T>) and dictionaries read from the definition and repetition levels of the file, the reverse of the shredding in 11b: the file's own nodes decide where objects and lists start (so required or optional groups, and the older list layouts, read the same), shapes that do not fit are SchemaMismatchExceptions, and only the nested columns the row type names are read. 12c Column types Done Refactor, no change in behavior: every .NET type that has a column of its own is a ColumnType<T> (Int32ColumnType, DateTimeColumnType, DecimalColumnType, EnumColumnType<T>, ...) holding all of its logic in one place: the column it creates, which columns of a file fit it, and the batch conversion to and from the physical type. The typed ReadBatch/WriteBatch overloads of the column reader and writer, and the serializer's shredders, assemblers and buffers, all use it; ColumnTypeRegistry finds them, and registering your own teaches the serializer a new type. Column attributes become ColumnSettings. 12d ADO.NET (IDataReader) Done ParquetDataWriter.Write/WriteAsync write the rows of any IDataReader as a Parquet file (column types from GetFieldType, nullability and decimal precision from the schema table, row groups of a set size, so memory is bounded), and ParquetDataReader is a DbDataReader over a Parquet file for SqlBulkCopy, DataTable.Load and the like: the top-level columns that hold one value per row, typed by their logical type, one row group in memory at a time. Nested columns are not exposed yet. Milestone 5 – Performance, extras, release # Step Status Deliverable 13 Performance pass (measure, strings) Done Comparison benchmarks against Parquet.Net and ParquetSharp (benchmarks/ParquetNeo.Benchmarks/Comparison), a per-column breakdown, and the string fast paths they led to: text dictionaries decoded once per entry, one-pass UTF-8 encoding, statistics of a dictionary column from its new entries only. Results and open items in PERFORMANCE.md. 13b Performance pass (serializer, parallelism) Done The serializer after the profile of step 13: columns of a row group encoded in parallel (MaxDegreeOfParallelism, same bytes whatever the degree), column buffers sized up front, a direct write to the stream, one delegate call per property, and lists and arrays sized from the file when reading (capped, since the file's numbers are not trusted). Serializer write 198 → 143 ms (128 ms with four threads), read 186 → 125 ms. 13c Performance pass (column writer) Done Writing through columns without allocating: dictionaries for numbers and byte arrays as open-addressing tables over pooled arrays, and pooled scratch buffers for the writer, both with the same bytes in the file. 52 MB → 18 KB allocated and 86 → 71 ms for the benchmark table; the unique-valued columns went from about 19 ms and 25 MB each to 5 and 12 ms and nothing. 13d Performance pass (the rest) Done One compiled function per object type instead of walking shredders and assemblers (done for flat rows, then for objects, collections and dictionaries inside rows; not yet for types built by a constructor), a public parallel form for the column API (done: RowGroupWriter.WriteColumns), faster string dictionaries (done: hash, ASCII, one loop), an earlier decision to give up a dictionary (done as the per-column DictionaryMode option), and asynchronous I/O tuning (done: a pooled staging area and the next row group encoded while the last is written). See PERFORMANCE.md. 14 Source generator Done AOT/trimming-safe DTO mapping replacing the reflection path; same tests run against both paths. Opt-in with [ParquetSerializable] on the DTO (or [assembly: ParquetSerializable(typeof(X))] for a type you do not own); the generator registers the mapping when the assembly loads, so Serialize<T>/Deserialize<T> stay as they are, and a type with no mapping keeps the reflection path, which is not trim or AOT safe. Done in small steps: 14a foundation, 14b flat rows, 14c nested rows and collections, 14d constructor-built types (all below). 14a AOT foundation (no generator yet) Done The library is IsAotCompatible with no warnings: column buffers and data are made through a visitor on ColumnType instead of MakeGenericType, enums are registered with ColumnTypeRegistry.RegisterEnum<T>() where types cannot be made at run time, the struct shredder and assembler take the function that shreds or builds a row instead of compiling it, and the reflection builders (the only code that reflects or compiles) are annotated RequiresUnreferencedCode/RequiresDynamicCode and refused under Native AOT with an explanation. RowModel<T>.Register/ReadModel<T>.Register is where a generated mapping plugs in. tests/ParquetNeo.AotSmoke is published with Native AOT in CI and runs the column API and the serializer (Gzip, Brotli) over a mapping written by hand, which the tests compare byte for byte with the reflection path. 14b Source generator (flat rows) Done ParquetNeo.Generator (a Roslyn incremental generator, netstandard2.0) and the public ParquetSerializableAttribute. For each marked type it writes straight-line shred and assemble code and registers it from a module initializer through MappingRegistry (the mapping itself is made the first time the serializer needs it): columns, their order, nullability (from the nullable annotations), enums, and the settings attributes (ParquetColumn, ParquetIgnore, ParquetDecimal, ParquetTime, ParquetTimestamp, ParquetEncoding, ParquetDictionary) all come out as the reflection path works them out. Types it cannot map yet (object, collection or dictionary properties, constructor-built types, generic or inaccessible types, attributes that do not suit their property) get warning PNEO001 and keep using reflection; a type that can be written but not read gets PNEO002. The runtime side is a small public surface (WriteMappingBuilder<T>, ReadMappingBuilder<T>, RowSink, RowSource) that wraps the internal shredders and assemblers. Tests: the generator's own project (output shape, diagnostics, the list of column types against the library's), and in ParquetNeo.Tests a type with every kind of column that gets a generated mapping next to a twin that does not, which must write byte-identical files and read the same rows. The Native AOT smoke test uses the generated mapping. Not yet: packaging the generator inside the ParquetNeo NuGet package (step 16). 14c Source generator (nested rows and collections) Done The generator maps objects and structs of any depth, and arrays, lists, sets, other ICollection<T>s and dictionaries of anything (including collections of collections, objects in dictionaries, nullable elements and values), each object type described once however often it is used. The public builders for generated code became stack-based (Leaf, BeginObject, BeginList/BeginNullableList, BeginMap/BeginMapOfNullable, End) over the same internal shredders and assemblers, so the schema, levels and messages are the ones of the reflection path; the generated straight-line code per object type reads its properties by column number relative to the object, since the object can be anywhere in the row. Collections that are not made from what was read (sets, collection classes) get a generated create function. Types it still leaves to reflection: constructor-built types (a type with an object like that inside can be written but not read, PNEO002), and the rest as in 14b. Tests: a row with every shape (objects and structs, nullable and not, lists, arrays, sets, collection classes, dictionaries, three levels deep, nulls and empties) written next to its reflection twin gives byte-identical files with several codecs and row-group sizes and the same rows and errors; the Native AOT smoke test round-trips a nested row with all of them. Speed against reflection (GeneratedMappingWriteBenchmarks, GeneratedMappingReadBenchmarks, flat and nested rows, see PERFORMANCE.md): the same within the error of the runs, with the same allocation. 14d Source generator (constructor-built types) Done A type without a public constructor without parameters (a record, a struct with get-only properties, a class with a constructor) is created by calling its public constructor that has the most parameters that are all properties of the same names (without regard to case) and types, as the reflection path chooses; the properties that are not parameters are set by their setters (init included) in the same expression. The generated code reads each parameter from its column straight into the call, with no boxed slots. A type with no constructor that fits (or an object inside it with none) can be written but not read, PNEO002. Tests: records with records, structs and lists inside, a class with several constructors and parameters of another case, a struct, and the message for a null in a parameter, each beside a reflection twin with byte-identical files; the Native AOT smoke test round-trips a record with a list of records. Reading a record with a generated mapping takes 20 ms against 47 ms for reflection (100,000 rows, 19 MB allocated against 35 MB), see PERFORMANCE.md. This completes step 14. 15 Read-side extras Done (15e deferred) Row-group skipping via statistics, page index, bloom filters, CRC32 page checksums, optional PAR3 / FlatBuffers footer; done in the parts below. 15a Row-group skipping Done ParquetFilter (Column("x").GreaterThan(5) & …; comparisons, Between, In, null tests, And/Or/Not) checked against the statistics of each row group by ParquetFileReader.GetMatchingRowGroups and RowGroupReader.MayMatch, and the RowGroupFilter option of ParquetSerializer (all four methods, the asynchronous ones do not fetch the bytes of a skipped row group) and ParquetDataReader. A filter only prunes: it never skips a row group with a row that satisfies it (checked against a plain evaluation of random data and filters), and the rows of the row groups it keeps are not filtered. Values compare as the column type defines (unsigned integers, decimals, dates, times and timestamps by their units, text by UTF-8 bytes, NaNs and nulls as in C#); enums and Guids only for equality; columns in collections, missing columns and missing statistics keep the row group. 15b LINQ over files Done ParquetNeo.Linq, a separate project (not AOT or trim safe: Open says so with attributes) with its own tests: ParquetDataset.Open<T>(path) gives an IQueryable<T> over a file or a directory of files (and the folders below it; local files). The expression tree is analyzed, and the rest is run by LINQ to objects over the rows that are read, so every operator keeps its meaning (OrderBy, GroupBy, Join with rows in memory, Distinct, Skip/Take, First*/Single*, aggregates, ...). What is added: the Wheres that come first are turned into a ParquetFilter (comparisons with constants and captured values, either side first, null tests, nullable HasValue, boolean properties, Contains on a list, nested properties, &&, ||, !; what cannot be turned is left out of an &&, and an || or ! is only turned when exact) that skips files and row groups from their footers while the whole predicate is applied to the rows read; a query that goes from the rows to something else with Select after only Where, ordering and paging reads only the columns it uses, through a class made at run time with just those properties (a row used whole, or any other operator before the Select, reads whole rows); Count(), LongCount() and Any() are answered from the footers; files are read in parallel (MaxDegreeOfParallelism), so without an OrderBy the rows come in no particular order; Explain() says which files, row groups and columns a query reads; AsAsyncEnumerable, ToListAsync, ToArrayAsync, FirstAsync, FirstOrDefaultAsync, CountAsync and AnyAsync run the query on another thread and do not block the caller. Also in this PR: ParquetFilter and FilterColumn moved to the ParquetNeo namespace. Tests: 69, including 150 random predicates over four files checked against the rows in memory, the conditions taken from predicates, the plans, directories, parallel reads, errors, and the async methods. 15c Checksums and bloom filters Done WritePageChecksums writes the CRC-32 of every page (after compression, slicing-by-8; checked against the standard test vector and gzip's trailer) in the page header; VerifyPageChecksums checks it on read and a mismatch is a CorruptColumnException that names the page. ColumnBloomFilters (by dotted column path, with BloomFilterSettings.FalsePositiveRate and MaxBytes) writes a split-block bloom filter per row group for the chosen columns (xxHash64, sized from the distinct count, after the columns of the row group); the filters are read lazily, and equality conditions (Equal, In, through And/Or/Not) use them to skip row groups the statistics cannot rule out, in GetMatchingRowGroups, the synchronous serializer, ADO.NET and LINQ. Not used: the asynchronous serializer (statistics only, to not fetch more ranges), zero, nanosecond times, floats not exactly representable, and booleans and INT96 cannot have one. Measured write cost (off by default): checksums +30-50% uncompressed and none with gzip; bloom filters +240-280% on unique columns uncompressed and none with gzip. Not verified: interop with files from other writers (no pyarrow here). 15d Page index Done WritePageIndex writes the OffsetIndex (where each data page is, its first row) and the ColumnIndex (smallest and largest value and null count of each page, unordered boundary order) of every column after the row groups, and records them in the column chunks; a column without bounds (values with no order, a page of only NaN, statistics off) gets only the offset index. RowGroupReader.SelectRows(filter, columns) cuts the row group where the pages of the columns the filter uses start and evaluates the filter with the bounds of the pages of each stretch (the same three-valued logic as for row groups, so And, Or and Not come for free), giving runs of rows (RowSelection); OpenColumn(index, selection) reads only those rows: pages with none are not read, a page with some is trimmed (by definition levels, repetition levels and plain, dictionary, boolean and delta encodings). Used by the synchronous serializer, ADO.NET reader and LINQ; the asynchronous serializer does not fetch the index. An index that does not fit its chunk is ignored. Measured (2M rows, one row group, 100 ids wanted): 313 ms to 39 ms uncompressed, 158 to 48 ms gzipped; the index is 2.5 KB of 63 MB and writing takes 8-10% longer, so it is off by default. Not done: binary search over ordered bounds (the writer states unordered), pages skipped by the asynchronous serializer, interop with files from other writers (not verified here). 15e PAR3 footer Deferred The PAR3 / FlatBuffers footer is still a proposal of the Parquet project (no adopted layout in a parquet-format release, no other reader to test against); do it when the format is adopted and readers support it. 16 Release Done README with examples, XML docs, NuGet packaging: eight packages with the version of the latest v tag (MinVer): ParquetNeo.Enums, ParquetNeo, ParquetNeo.Serialization (with the source generator as an analyzer), ParquetNeo.Linq, ParquetNeo.Compression.{Snappy,Lz4,Zstd}, and ParquetNeo.All, which has no code and depends on all of them. CI packs them and installs ParquetNeo.All in a new Native AOT program (build/verify-packages.sh); a v* tag publishes to nuget.org with Trusted Publishing (no API key) and makes a GitHub release. Public members without XML docs are not errors yet. 17 Preview & new types Planned ALP encoding, then Variant / Variant shredding and Geospatial (GEOMETRY/GEOGRAPHY). Possible enhancements after step 15, not planned in detail: Hive-style partition folders (year=2024/month=05/…) as virtual columns of ParquetDataset<T>, so that a filter on them skips whole files without opening them. A storage abstraction (listing files and opening a stream or a byte range of one) so that datasets can be read from blob storage as well as from local files; the datasets use local files until then. Steps 0–7b are the minimum for flat tables, 8 and 8b are needed for real-world files, and 11–12 deliver the DTO API. Steps 13–15 may be reordered based on benchmark results. Testing Framework: TUnit. Every library project has a test project of its own (tests/<Project>.Tests: ParquetNeo.Tests, ParquetNeo.Serialization.Tests, ParquetNeo.Enums.Tests, ParquetNeo.Compression.Snappy.Tests, ...), with the fixtures it needs in its own Fixtures folder. Test code that several of them share (the checks every codec must pass, the data they run on) is in tests/ParquetNeo.Tests.Common, a library with no tests. A test belongs to the project of the code it is about; a test that exercises several projects together (the writer with every codec, for example) lives with the project that uses the others. Unit tests for every encoder/decoder: golden-byte vectors from the spec, edge cases (empty, single value, run boundaries, bit widths 0–64), and randomized round-trips. Write → read round-trip tests for every physical/logical type, encoding and codec. Interop tests: read files produced by other implementations (apache/parquet-testing), and where tooling allows, verify files we write with an independent reader. Allocation tests on hot paths (e.g. asserting no allocations per value). TreatWarningsAsErrors stays on; CI runs build + tests on every PR.

api/ParquetNeo.ColumnWriter.html.summary: Class ColumnWriter Namespace ParquetNeo Assembly ParquetNeo.dll Writes the values of one column of a row group. Obtain it from NextColumn(), call one of the Write… methods one or more times, then move on to the next column. public sealed class ColumnWriter Inheritance object ColumnWriter Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks For a required column pass only the values. For an optional column also pass one definition level per row: 0 for a null and 1 for a value, with values holding just the non-null values in order. A nested column (a leaf below optional or repeated groups) has a definition level per entry that counts how many of its optional and repeated ancestors, and itself, are present, up to MaxDefinitionLevel: only entries at that level carry a value. A column inside a repeated group also takes a repetition level per entry, which says at which repeated ancestor the entry repeats: 0 starts a new row, and a higher level continues the row at that depth. Entries are the unit of a batch; a row can span several entries and even several batches (it ends where the next entry with repetition level 0 begins), and the first entry of a column must start a row. Pages never end in the middle of a row. The levels are checked against their ranges but not against the schema's structure: levels that no row could produce give a file readers will reject. Values are buffered into pages of about DataPageSize bytes, which are compressed and written to the stream as they fill. Instances are not thread safe. That saves filling a dictionary that would be dropped anyway, which is much of the time of such a column, and the larger file. A column that repeats only after its first values has no dictionary. Standard = 0 Every distinct value goes into a dictionary until the dictionary passes ParquetWriterOptions.DictionaryPageSizeLimit, and then the rest of the column is written plain. api/ParquetNeo.Nested.ColumnStructure.ht.summary: Class ColumnStructure Namespace ParquetNeo.Nested Assembly ParquetNeo.dll The shape of the data in one column, as validity and offsets instead of definition and repetition levels: for each optional node on the way to the column whether its value is present, and for each repeated node where each list starts and ends. It is the columnar form of nested data (the same idea as the validity and offsets of an Arrow array), and it converts both ways with the levels the reader returns and the writer takes. public sealed class ColumnStructure Inheritance object ColumnStructure Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Only the nodes that can be missing or repeated take part; required nodes add nothing. The Levels come outermost first. Every level has one entry per item of its depth: depth 0 has one item per row, and the items of depth d are the elements of the d-th repeated level. Where an ancestor is missing, the entries of the optional levels below it (at the same depth) say false and a repeated level below it says an empty list. The values of the column are not part of the structure: they are the values of the entries whose every ancestor is present, in order, which is exactly what ColumnWriter takes and ColumnReader returns. articles/ado-net.html.title: ADO.NET | ParquetNeo
articles/ado-net.html.summary: ADO.NET Write the rows of any IDataReader (a database query, DataTable.CreateDataReader(), ...) as a Parquet file, and read a Parquet file as a DbDataReader, which works with SqlBulkCopy, DataTable.Load and the like. This is in the ParquetNeo package. using ParquetNeo.Data; using var query = command.ExecuteReader(); using var output = File.Create("orders.parquet"); ParquetDataWriter.Write(query, output); using var input = File.OpenRead("orders.parquet"); using var reader = new ParquetDataReader(input); while (reader.Read()) { Console.WriteLine($"{reader.GetInt64(0)} {reader.GetString(1)}"); } The writer takes the type of each column from GetFieldType, and the nullability and the precision of decimals from the schema table of the reader. It writes row groups of a set size, so memory does not depend on the number of rows. WriteAsync is the asynchronous version. ParquetDataReaderOptions chooses which columns to read, and takes a filter that skips row groups and pages that cannot hold the rows you want: see Skipping what is not needed.

articles/aot.html.title: Trimming and Native AOT | ParquetNeo
articles/aot.html.summary: Trimming and Native AOT ParquetNeo and ParquetNeo.Serialization are trim and Native AOT safe (IsAotCompatible). ParquetNeo.Linq is not: it builds expression trees and types at run time. By default the serializer finds out how a type maps to columns by reflection and compiles that into code the first time the type is used, which neither trimming nor Native AOT allows. The source generator, which comes with the ParquetNeo.Serialization package, writes the mapping when you build, so nothing is looked at or compiled at run time. using ParquetNeo.DataModel; [ParquetSerializable] public sealed class Order { public long Id { get; set; } public string? Name { get; set; } public double Total { get; set; } } For a type you do not own, put the attribute on the assembly: [assembly: ParquetSerializable(typeof(TheirType))] The serializer is called as before, and uses the generated mapping when there is one. What the generator handles Properties that are single columns (numbers, strings, dates, Guid, enums, byte arrays and their nullable forms), objects and structs nested to any depth, and arrays, lists, sets and dictionaries of any of them. A type created with a constructor without parameters is read with the setters of its properties; one without, such as a record, is read by calling its constructor with the values of the properties it names. What it does when it cannot For a type it cannot map (a property of a type that is not stored as columns, or no constructor that fits) the generator reports a warning at build time, and the type keeps working through reflection. A type it can write but not read gets a warning of its own. In a Native AOT program a type with no generated mapping is refused, with an explanation of why. Checking it The repository publishes a small program with Native AOT in its CI, and checks the packages by installing ParquetNeo.All in a new program published the same way.

articles/compression.html.title: Compression | ParquetNeo
articles/compression.html.summary: Compression Gzip and Brotli are built in. Snappy, LZ4_RAW and Zstandard are in separate packages so that you only get the libraries you use. A codec is registered in the CodecRegistry that the options use, and chosen by ParquetWriterOptions.Compression: using ParquetNeo.Compression; using ParquetNeo.Compression.Zstd; using ParquetNeo.Serialization; var codecs = new CodecRegistry().AddZstd(level: 3); ParquetSerializer.Serialize(rows, stream, new ParquetSerializerOptions { Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions { Compression = CompressionCodec.Zstd, Codecs = codecs }, }); var back = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Row>(stream, new ParquetDeserializerOptions { Reader = new ParquetReaderOptions { Codecs = codecs }, }); Codec Package Register with Gzip, Brotli ParquetNeo already registered Snappy ParquetNeo.Compression.Snappy AddSnappy() LZ4_RAW ParquetNeo.Compression.Lz4 AddLz4Raw() Zstandard ParquetNeo.Compression.Zstd AddZstd(level) LZ4 with the Hadoop framing and LZO are not supported. LZ4_RAW is. Pages are compressed one by one, so a reader can skip the pages and the row groups it does not need without decompressing them.

articles/filtering.html.title: Skipping what is not needed | ParquetNeo
articles/filtering.html.summary: Skipping what is not needed The fastest way to read a big file is to not read most of it. A file has several levels of information that tell a reader what a part of it holds, and a ParquetFilter is checked against them: Level What it records Written by default Rules out Row group statistics the smallest and largest value of each column of the row group, and how many are null yes whole row groups Page index the same for every page of a column, and where the page is no (WritePageIndex) pages inside a row group Bloom filters whether a value is certainly not in the column of a row group no (ColumnBloomFilters) row groups, for equality conditions Page checksums a CRC-32 of every page no (WritePageChecksums) nothing: they detect damaged pages Filters using ParquetNeo; var recent = ParquetFilter.Column("Born").GreaterThanOrEqual(new DateOnly(1900, 1, 1)) & ParquetFilter.Column("Name").IsNotNull(); A filter is made of comparisons (Equal, NotEqual, GreaterThan, ..., Between, In), null tests, and And (&), Or (|) and Not (!). Important A filter only prunes. It rules out what cannot match, and the rows of what it keeps are all returned, including rows that do not satisfy it. Apply the condition to the rows as well when the result must be exact. (ParquetNeo.Linq does that for you.) Using them var rows = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(stream, new ParquetDeserializerOptions { RowGroupFilter = recent }); ParquetDataReaderOptions.RowGroupFilter is the same for the ADO.NET reader, and ParquetFileReader.GetMatchingRowGroups(filter) tells you which row groups of a file may match. The row groups that are ruled out are not read. The asynchronous methods of ParquetSerializer do not even fetch their bytes, but they only use the statistics: they do not fetch the page index or the bloom filters. The page index A row group is made of many pages, and its statistics say nothing of which of them hold a value. With a page index, a filter skips pages as well as row groups: var options = new ParquetSerializerOptions { Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions { WritePageIndex = true } }; It pays when the values of a column are in some order (a time, an id that grows), which makes the bounds of a page tight. Reading 100 ids out of 2 million in one row group took 313 ms with the statistics of the row group only and 39 ms with the page index (158 and 48 ms with gzip). The index took 2.5 KB of a 63 MB file, and writing took 8 to 10% longer. At the low level, RowGroupReader.SelectRows(filter, columns) returns the rows to read as a RowSelection, and OpenColumn(index, selection) reads only those rows: the pages with none of them are not read. Bloom filters Statistics rule out little when values are spread widely (ids, names, e-mail addresses): every row group has a smallest and a largest value that bracket what you look for. A bloom filter says that a value is certainly not in a row group, or that it may be (with a small chance of a wrong "may be", the false positive rate). var written = new ParquetSerializerOptions { Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions { ColumnBloomFilters = new Dictionary<string, BloomFilterSettings> { ["Email"] = new() { FalsePositiveRate = 0.01 } }, }, }; var found = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(stream, new ParquetDeserializerOptions { RowGroupFilter = ParquetFilter.Column("Email").Equal("ada@example.com"), }); A filter takes room in the file: about a byte for every few different values. Writing the column takes several times as long when its pages are not compressed, and a little longer when they are. Bloom filters in files written by other tools are read too. Page checksums var written = new ParquetWriterOptions { WritePageChecksums = true }; var read = new ParquetReaderOptions { VerifyPageChecksums = true }; // a damaged page throws CorruptColumnException Computing the checksum costs about a second per GB of page bytes.

articles/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started Install dotnet add package ParquetNeo.All This installs everything. To take less, see Packages. Write and read rows Each public property of a class or record becomes a column. Nested objects, lists and dictionaries work too. using ParquetNeo.Serialization; var people = new List<Person> { new(1, "Ada", new DateOnly(1815, 12, 10)), new(2, "Alan", new DateOnly(1912, 6, 23)), new(3, "Grace", new DateOnly(1906, 12, 9)), }; using (var file = File.Create("people.parquet")) { ParquetSerializer.Serialize(people, file); } using var input = File.OpenRead("people.parquet"); List<Person> back = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(input); public record Person(int Id, string Name, DateOnly Born); There are asynchronous versions of both (SerializeAsync, DeserializeAsync, and DeserializeAllAsync for an IAsyncEnumerable<T>), and DeserializeAll reads one row group at a time so that a big file does not have to fit in memory. articles/linq.html.title: LINQ over files | ParquetNeo
articles/linq.html.summary: LINQ over files ParquetNeo.Linq queries a file, or all the files of a directory (and the folders below it), with LINQ. It is not trim or Native AOT safe: it reads expression trees and builds types at run time. using ParquetNeo.Linq; var people = ParquetDataset.Open<Person>("people/"); var names = people.Where(p => p.Born >= new DateOnly(1900, 1, 1) && p.Name != null) .OrderBy(p => p.Born) .Select(p => new { p.Name, p.Born }) .Take(100) .ToList(); ParquetDataset<T> is an IQueryable<T>. Every operator of LINQ to objects works on the rows that are read, and what is added is what lets it read less: Files, row groups and pages are skipped. The Wheres at the start of the query are turned into a ParquetFilter (see Skipping what is not needed): comparisons with constants and captured values, null tests, boolean properties, Contains on a list, nested properties, &&, || and !. The whole predicate is still applied to the rows that are read, so the result is exact. Only the columns a query uses are read, when it ends in a Select after only Wheres, ordering and paging. Count(), LongCount() and Any() are answered from the footers of the files when they can be. Files are read in parallel, so without an OrderBy the rows come in no particular order. var plan = people.Where(p => p.Id > 5000).Explain(); // which files and row groups are skipped, which columns are read int count = people.Count(); // from the footers: no data is read await foreach (var row in people.Where(p => p.Id > 5000).AsAsyncEnumerable()) { } AsAsyncEnumerable, ToListAsync, ToArrayAsync, FirstAsync, FirstOrDefaultAsync, CountAsync and AnyAsync run the query on another thread and do not block the caller. Datasets are local files for now.

articles/low-level.html.title: Low-level API | ParquetNeo
articles/low-level.html.summary: Low-level API The low-level API (package ParquetNeo) works on row groups and column chunks, with Span<T> and definition and repetition levels. The serializer is built on it. Writing Describe the columns in a schema, then write one batch of values per column for each row group: using ParquetNeo; using ParquetNeo.Metadata; using ParquetNeo.Schema; var schema = new ParquetSchema( [ new PrimitiveNode("id", PhysicalType.Int64, FieldRepetitionType.Required), new PrimitiveNode("name", PhysicalType.ByteArray, FieldRepetitionType.Required, LogicalType.String), ]); using var file = File.Create("people.parquet"); using var writer = new ParquetFileWriter(file, schema); using (var group = writer.AppendRowGroup()) { group.NextColumn().WriteBatch([1L, 2L, 3L]); group.NextColumn().WriteStrings(["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"]); } With several columns, WriteColumns encodes them on different threads and makes the same file (it holds the encoded group in memory until all columns are done): using (var group = writer.AppendRowGroup()) { group.WriteColumns( [ column => column.WriteBatch([1L, 2L, 3L]), column => column.WriteStrings(["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"]), ]); } The footer is written when the writer is disposed. Reading using var reader = new ParquetFileReader(stream); var group = reader.OpenRowGroup(0); using var column = group.OpenColumn("id"); var values = new long[1000]; BatchRead read; while ((read = column.ReadBatch(values)).Entries > 0) { // use values[..read.Entries] } An optional column also takes a span for its definition levels: it receives 0 for a null and the maximum level for a value, and values receives only the values that are not null, packed at the start. A column in a list also takes the repetition levels. Memory is bounded by the largest page: pages are read one at a time and their buffers come from a pool. Statistics and metadata RowGroupReader.GetStatistics gives the smallest and largest value and the null count of a column, as .NET values, and ParquetFileReader.Metadata is the footer: the schema, the row groups and their column chunks. Safety limits ParquetReaderOptions has limits that bound what a corrupt or hostile file can make the reader allocate (for example MaxPageSize). A damaged file throws a ParquetException that says what is wrong.

articles/serializer.html.title: Serializing your classes | ParquetNeo
articles/serializer.html.summary: Serializing your classes ParquetSerializer (package ParquetNeo.Serialization) writes the properties of your classes and records as columns and reads them back. using ParquetNeo.Serialization; ParquetSerializer.Serialize(rows, stream, new ParquetSerializerOptions { RowGroupSize = 100_000, // rows in a row group: the unit that is read, skipped, and compressed together MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4, // columns of a row group are encoded on this many threads; the bytes do not depend on it Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions { Compression = CompressionCodec.Gzip }, }); What maps to a column Single columns: numbers, decimal, bool, strings, byte arrays, Guid, the date and time types (DateOnly, TimeOnly, DateTime, DateTimeOffset), enums, and the nullable forms of those. Around them: Nested objects and structs, to any depth, become groups. Arrays, lists, sets and other collections become LIST columns, and dictionaries become MAPs. A property is optional (it may be null in the file) when its type is nullable: int?, string? with nullable reference types on, and so on. Records and classes with a constructor that has parameters are read by calling that constructor with the values of the properties it names. The columns are matched with the properties by name when reading, so the file may have more columns than the class, and a column that the class does not have is not read. Adjusting the mapping Attributes in ParquetNeo.DataModel change how a property is stored: Attribute Effect [ParquetColumn("name")] The name of the column, or its position among the columns [ParquetIgnore] The property is not written or read [ParquetDecimal(precision, scale)] The precision and scale of a decimal (the default is 38 and 18) [ParquetTime(unit)], [ParquetTimestamp(...)] The unit and meaning of the column of a time or of a date and time [ParquetEncoding(encoding)] The encoding of the values of the column (PLAIN by default) [ParquetDictionary(mode)] Whether the column has a dictionary: on, off, or decided by what the values look like Reading a big file Deserialize returns a list. DeserializeAll and DeserializeAllAsync give the rows one row group at a time, so memory is bounded by the largest row group: foreach (var row in ParquetSerializer.DeserializeAll<Person>(stream)) { // ... } To read less of the file, give a filter: see Skipping what is not needed.

index.html.summary: ParquetNeo A high-performance .NET library for reading and writing Apache Parquet files. Fast: span-based, allocation-conscious, SIMD where it pays off. See Performance. Two layers: a low-level API on row groups and column chunks, and a high-level API that reads and writes your classes and records. Skips what it does not need: filters rule out row groups and pages by their statistics, page index and bloom filters; queries read only the columns they use. Trim and Native AOT safe: a source generator writes the mapping of your types at build time. Minimal dependencies: the core depends only on the BCL; the codecs that need a library are separate packages. dotnet add package ParquetNeo.All using ParquetNeo.Serialization; using var file = File.Create("people.parquet"); ParquetSerializer.Serialize(people, file); var back = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(File.OpenRead("people.parquet")); public record Person(int Id, string Name, DateOnly Born); Start with Getting started, or go to the API reference.
